summary: Gives an analysis of one method of choosing among equal-cost paths in equal-cost multi-path routing.

plainLanguage.summary: When a router has several paths of equal cost to the same destination, it has to choose one for each packet. RFC 2992 studies one method for making that choice, checks how much work it takes, and measures how much traffic has to move when the set of paths changes.

questions: how much disruption does hash threshold cause
how does ecmp choose a next hop
subtitle: How a router picks one of several equal-cost paths, and what that choice costs when the paths change

tldr.problem: A router with several equal-cost paths to the same destination must pick one next-hop for each packet, and the way it picks has to be cheap to compute and stable for each flow.
tldr.mechanism: The memo analyses hash-threshold: the router hashes the header fields that identify a flow into a key, and each next-hop owns a region of that key space, so the region containing the key decides the next-hop.
tldr.outcome: The lookup is constant time, but adding or removing a next-hop moves between a quarter and a half of all flows to a different path. The memo compares this with modulo-N and highest random weight, and recommends adding new regions in the centre rather than at the ends.

facts.label: Hash used in the example
facts.value: CRC16 over the flow-defining header fields

today: RFC 2992 is an Informational memo that has not been obsoleted or updated. It is an analysis rather than a specification, so it defines no protocol; its formulas are a reference for anyone deciding how a router should choose among equal-cost paths.

sections.title: The Hash-Threshold Algorithm
sections.content:
Equal-cost multi-path (ECMP) routing sends packets along several paths that cost the same. The forwarding engine identifies the paths by next-hop, so the router has to choose one next-hop for each packet.

The memo analyses one way of making that choice, called hash-threshold. The router first hashes the header fields that identify a flow, for example the source and destination fields, and uses the result as a key. The N next-hops have each been given a unique region of that key space, and the router picks the next-hop whose region contains the key.

In the memo's example the hash is a CRC16 and there are four next-hops. The key space is 16 bits wide, so for equal usage each region is 65536/4, or 16k, of the space. The next-hop is chosen by finding the region that contains the hash result.
sections.plainLanguage: When a router has several equally good paths to the same place, it has to pick one for each packet. This memo studies a method that picks the path by turning the packet's flow details into a number and looking that number up in a table of paths. The same flow always gets the same path, unless the table changes.

sections.title: The Cost of Choosing a Path
sections.content:
The memo splits the work into three parts: choosing the regions for the next-hops, computing the key, and comparing the key with the regions to find the next-hop.

Because the regions are required to be of equal size, the boundaries are trivial to work out. Each boundary sits exactly one region size away from the previous one, starting from zero for the first region, and the memo notes that for equal-sized regions the boundary values do not need to be stored at all.

Finding the next-hop is then a single division. The lookup is O(1) when the next-hops are held in an array indexed by region, so the time taken depends on how the next-hops are laid out in memory. The hash function is not specified, so its cost is whatever the chosen function costs, and the memo notes it can be done in hardware in parallel with the other work that has to finish before a next-hop can be chosen.
sections.plainLanguage: Working out which path to use has three steps: set up the ranges for each path, compute the number from the packet, and find the range that number falls in. Because all the ranges are the same size, the last step is a single division, and a router can look up the answer in constant time. The memo does not pick the hash function, so that cost is left to the implementer.

sections.title: How Much a Change Disrupts
sections.content:
Protocols such as TCP behave better when the path a flow uses does not change while the connection lasts. The memo measures disruption as the fraction of total flows whose path changes in response to some change in the router. This matters when one of the paths is flapping.

Some algorithms, such as round-robin, are disruptive whatever happens, because a flow moves to the least recently used next-hop on every packet. Hash-threshold is not: as long as the region boundaries do not move, the same next-hop is chosen for a given flow.

With equal-sized regions the boundaries move only when a next-hop is added or removed, and then every region has to grow or shrink to fill the key space. The memo works through two examples with five regions: deleting region 3 gives a disruption of 3/10, and deleting region 4 gives 7/20. The general formula built from those examples leads to three results. The least disruption comes when the removed region is as close to the middle as possible, which reduces to 1/4 + 1/(4*N). The most disruption comes when an edge region is removed, which reduces to 1/2. The range of possible disruption is therefore (1/4, 1/2]. To keep disruption low, the memo recommends adding new regions to the centre rather than the ends.
sections.plainLanguage: When the set of available paths changes, some traffic has to be sent somewhere different, and a running connection notices that. The memo measures how much traffic has to move. Removing a path from the middle of the range moves about a quarter of the traffic. Removing one from the very end moves about half. The advice is to add new paths in the middle, not at the edges.

sections.title: Comparison With Other Choices
sections.content:
The memo compares hash-threshold with two other methods that do not move traffic around on their own, which rules out round-robin and random choice. Modulo-N runs the flow-defining header fields through a hash function and applies a final modulo-N to the result, which then maps directly to a next-hop. It performs as well as hash-threshold but is the most disruptive of the three: adding or removing a next-hop disrupts (N-1)/N of flows.

Highest random weight (HRW) is closer to hash-threshold with regions of differing sizes. For each next-hop the router seeds a pseudo-random number generator with the flow fields and the next-hop to obtain a weight, and the next-hop with the highest weight is selected. HRW has the least disruption, always 1/N, but its lookup is O(N), which is more expensive than the O(1) of the other two methods.

The memo says HRW is worth considering when its cost is acceptable, for example where per-flow state is kept and the next-hop choice is made infrequently. When it is too expensive, hash-threshold is the obvious choice, since it performs as well as modulo-N and is less disruptive.
sections.plainLanguage: Two other methods are compared. Modulo-N takes the remainder of a number to pick a path; it is fast but sends half or more of the traffic somewhere new when the paths change. Highest random weight scores every path and takes the best; it moves the least traffic but costs more work per packet. The memo suggests the expensive one where choices are rare, and the fast one where they are not.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says that its analysis of an algorithm used to make an ECMP routing decision does not directly affect the security of the Internet infrastructure. It makes no other security statement.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says that choosing between equal-cost paths has no security effect on the Internet. It makes no other comment on security.
